intermediate.description: Training regularly for a year or more.

advanced.label: Advanced
advanced.description: Years of consistent training, races done.

reference.title: How fast do you run right now?
reference.hint: A recent race result gives the most accurate pace zones.

easyPace.title: Your easy pace
easyPace.hint: The pace you can run while still talking in full sentences.

hoursPerWeek.title: How many hours do you ride per week?
hoursPerWeek.hint: On average over the last months, including commuting.

powerMeter.title: Do you ride with a power meter or smart trainer?

longest.title: Your longest ride of the last few weeks

learning.label: I can’t swim 100 m without a break
learning.description: We start with technique and short sets.

can100.label: I can swim 100 m without a break

comfortable.label: I swim comfortably
comfortable.description: 400 m and more without a break.

time400.title: 400 m time (optional)
time400.hint: Your best recent all-out 400 m. Together with a 200 m time it sets your swim zones (CSS).

time200.title: 200 m time (optional)
time200.hint: All-out 200 m, swum after a recovery. Leave it empty if you don’t know – a test session follows in the plan.

longest.title: Your longest swim of the last few weeks
longest.hint: One number is enough. Your plan never starts below it.

resting.title: Resting heart rate (optional)
resting.hint: Measure in the morning before getting up: count your pulse for 60 seconds, or use your watch’s resting value. It makes your zones more personal.

max.title: Max heart rate (optional)
max.hint: The highest value your watch showed at the end of an all-out effort, e.g. a hill sprint. If you leave it empty, we estimate it from your age.

availability.title: How much time do you have each day?
availability.hint: Set a typical week. You can change single weeks later, e.g. when travelling.

doubles.title: Can you train twice on one day?
doubles.hint: E.g. a swim in the morning and a run in the evening. Never two hard sessions.

terrain.title: What is the terrain like where you train?

disclaimer.title: Before you start
disclaimer.text: Peakr gives general training guidance and is not medical advice. If you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, are pregnant, take medication or have any other health concern, talk to your doctor before starting. Stop training and get help if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual shortness of breath.
disclaimer.confirm: I have read this and train at my own responsibility.

insights.title: Good to know
insights.zone2: Your Zone 2 is {{min}}–{{max}} bpm. Most of your training happens here – easy enough to talk, hard enough to build your engine.
insights.zone2Estimate: Your Zone 2 is about {{min}}–{{max}} bpm (estimated from your age). Most of your training happens here. You can refine it anytime in Profile → Training zones.

goal.triathlon: Triathlon plans start with roughly {{swim}} % swim, {{bike}} % bike and {{run}} % run – adjusted to your week.
goal.race: For this race at least {{weeks}} weeks of preparation are recommended. Your plan builds up in phases and tapers before race day.
goal.weightloss: Training supports weight loss best together with nutrition: easy sessions you can keep up, plus strength to keep muscle.
goal.fitness: Your plan loops build and recovery blocks, so you keep getting fitter without burning out.

run.threshold: Your threshold pace is about {{pace}} /km – the pace you could hold for about an hour. Your pace zones are based on it.
run.thresholdFromEasy: From your easy pace we estimate a threshold pace of about {{pace}} /km. A test run in the plan will make it precise.
run.noReference: No problem – your runs are guided by heart rate, and a short test run in the plan sets your pace zones.

swim.css: Your Critical Swim Speed is {{pace}} /100 m. Swim sets are prescribed relative to it.
swim.noTimes: Your swim sets start with standard paces; a CSS test in the plan makes them personal.
swim.technique: We start with technique and short intervals, so you can swim longer without a break soon.

insights.availability: You have {{days}} training days and up to {{hours}} hours per week. The plan uses less at the start and builds up gradually – never more than 10 % per week.

targetDate.ok: {{weeks}} weeks until race day – enough for a full build-up ({{recommended}} weeks recommended).
targetDate.short: Only {{weeks}} weeks until race day – {{recommended}} are recommended, so your plan is compressed. Getting to the start healthy comes first.
targetDate.none: No race date yet: your plan runs {{weeks}} weeks – the recommended preparation – and ends with a taper. Add the date later and the plan adapts.

barriers.time: Busy weeks happen: you can rebuild a single week in seconds and the plan keeps your training load.
barriers.motivation: Each session tells you why it matters, and you see your progress week by week.
barriers.injury: Your load grows at most 10 % per week, with a recovery week every 3–4 weeks and never two hard days in a row.
barriers.knowledge: Every session comes with clear targets – heart-rate zone, duration and structure.
barriers.rigid: Move sessions anytime: the week rebalances itself and warns you if two hard days end up back to back.
barriers.boredom: Your plan mixes sports, terrain and session types – and winter sports count too.
barriers.none: Great starting point. Let’s build a plan that keeps it that way.

insights.weightloss: A safe pace is at most {{kg}} kg per week (1 % of your body weight). Your training plan supports it; nutrition tracking comes with the Training + Nutrition plan.
insights.commute: Your commute adds about {{hours}} h of easy training on {{days}} days a week. It counts towards your plan, so the other sessions fit around it.
insights.winter: From December to March your plan offers winter variants of your easy and long sessions – with the same training load. You can change the winter period anytime.

forecast.loadHint: Every sport and strength count towards one load. Lighter bars are recovery weeks.
forecast.chartLabel: Weekly training load over {{weeks}} weeks, from {{from}} in week 1 up to {{max}}.
forecast.basis: Calculated by the Peakr training engine from your answers – no guesses.
forecast.buildRoutinesHint: Strength is scheduled once you have built a routine.
forecast.lockedTitle: {{weeks}} more weeks are ready for you
forecast.trial: Start your 7-day free trial and use everything right away: the full plan, workout tracking and feedback, and all integrations. You pay only after 7 days – cancel anytime before.

outcome.volume: Your weekly training time grows from {{from}} h to {{to}} h over {{weeks}} weeks.
outcome.racePrediction: Your {{reference}} time predicts {{time}} for the {{distance}} today – your plan builds from there.
outcome.raceCurrent: Your current {{distance}} time is {{time}} – your plan builds from there.
outcome.threshold: Your runs are paced from a threshold pace of {{pace}} /km.
outcome.css: Your swim sets are paced from a CSS of {{pace}} /100 m.
outcome.easyShare: About {{percent}} % of your endurance time is easy – the 80/20 rule that builds fitness without burnout.
outcome.oneLoad: All your sports share one load budget: a hard ride makes the next run easier automatically.
outcome.weightloss: Safe weight-loss pace: at most {{kg}} kg per week.
outcome.routinesPending: Strength from your own routines is added once you have built one.

sport.hint: Riding, running or walking to work counts as easy training – we plan it first.

notes.benchmark: Test week: this session updates your zones.
notes.downgraded: Planned {{type}} session made easy – it did not fit your available time without two hard days in a row.
notes.intensityBalance: Planned {{type}} session made easy to keep about 80 % of your training easy.
notes.loadCap: Shortened so this week does not increase the training load by more than 10 %.
notes.loadCapEasy: Planned {{type}} session made shorter and easy so this week does not increase the load by more than 10 %.
notes.recoveryWeek: Recovery week – less load so your body can absorb the training.
notes.taperWeek: Taper – less volume, some sharpness, fresh legs for race day.
notes.shortPreparation: Only {{weeks}} weeks until your race – {{recommended}} weeks are recommended, so the plan is compressed.
notes.strengthMerged: Not enough free days for your split: sessions are combined into {{sessions}}.
notes.strengthNoDay: No free day for strength this week.
notes.strengthSkipped: The {{type}} strength session did not fit this week without hurting a key session.
notes.noRaceDate: No race date yet – your plan runs the recommended {{weeks}} weeks. Add the date anytime and the plan adapts.
notes.eased: Made easier: the planned {{type}} session is now easy, so you do not have two hard days in a row.
notes.commuteNoRoom: A commute does not fit the time you have on one day this week, so it is not planned there. Add minutes for that day to count it.
notes.weekOverride: This week is different – rebuilt for the time you have.
notes.travelWeek: Travel week – hotel-room strength, runs by time and alternatives for rides and swims.
notes.travelStrength: Travel: bodyweight and band exercises you can do in a hotel room.
notes.travelReplaced: Travel: the planned {{type}} session is replaced by an easy session of similar load you can do there.
notes.travelDropped: Travel: the planned {{type}} session has no alternative at your travel location.
notes.absorbed: Shorter: an extra {{minutes}}-minute activity this week already covers part of the load.

run.recovery: Very easy running helps your legs recover from the last hard session.
run.easy: Easy Zone 2 running builds your aerobic engine – the base of every plan.
run.easyStrides: An easy run with a few short, relaxed strides keeps your legs quick without tiring you.
run.long: The long run builds endurance and teaches your body to run efficiently for longer.
run.uphillHike: Steep hiking and running builds the climbing strength mountain events demand.
run.progression: Starting easy and finishing faster teaches pacing and builds fitness without a hard interval session.
run.fartlek: Playful surges by feel – a gentle introduction to faster running that works on any terrain.
run.hillsShort: Short hill sprints build power and running economy with low injury risk.
run.hillsLong: Longer hill repeats build strength endurance at threshold effort.
run.tempo: Threshold running raises the pace you can hold for a long time.
run.vo2: Intervals at VO2max pace raise your aerobic ceiling.
run.racePace: Running at goal race pace makes that pace feel familiar and controlled on race day.
run.downhill: Controlled descents prepare your legs for the eccentric load of downhill racing.
run.commute: Running to work counts as easy training – it is part of the plan.

bike.recovery: An easy spin with high cadence flushes your legs after hard days.
bike.endurance: Steady Zone 2 riding builds aerobic fitness with little fatigue.
bike.long: The long ride builds the endurance you need for long days in the saddle.
bike.commute: Your commute counts as easy training – it is part of the plan.
bike.tempo: Steady tempo efforts build muscular endurance.
bike.sweetspot: Sweet-spot intervals give a lot of fitness for the time invested.
bike.threshold: Threshold intervals raise the power you can sustain for an hour.
bike.vo2: Short, hard intervals raise your maximum aerobic power.
bike.climb: Climbing efforts build strength on the bike and prepare you for hilly routes.
bike.cadence: Cadence drills improve pedalling efficiency inside an easy ride.

swim.technique: Drills improve your stroke – in swimming, technique is the fastest way to get faster.
swim.aerobic: Steady aerobic swimming builds endurance in the water.
swim.easy: Easy continuous swimming keeps the feel for the water without extra fatigue.
swim.css: Repeats at your Critical Swim Speed raise the pace you can hold over distance.
swim.speed: Short fast repeats with long rest build speed and a strong stroke.
swim.openwater: Sighting and continuous swimming prepare you for open-water racing.

why.brick: Running straight off the bike teaches your legs the transition you will feel on race day.

winter.xcski: Cross-country skiing builds the same aerobic fitness – with less impact on your legs.
winter.xcskiIntervals: Intervals on skis train your threshold while giving your running legs a break.
winter.skitour: Ski touring builds climbing endurance; the ascent is the training.
winter.snowshoe: Snowshoeing is a low-impact, full-body endurance session.

benchmark.run5k: A 5 km time trial updates your pace zones and race prediction.
benchmark.run30: A 30-minute solo effort measures your threshold heart rate (average of the last 20 minutes).
benchmark.swimCss: A 400 m and 200 m time trial updates your Critical Swim Speed.
benchmark.bikeFtp: A 20-minute test estimates your FTP (about 95 % of the average power).

strength.peakrBase: General strength now makes you more robust for the harder endurance weeks ahead.
strength.peakrBuild: Heavy, low-rep strength and jumps make you more economical and powerful.
strength.peakrPeak: A short maintenance session keeps your strength while the endurance work peaks.
strength.coreMobility: Core and mobility work keeps you moving well without tiring your legs.
strength.fullBody: A full-body session from your split.
strength.upper: Upper-body work from your split – it does not tire your legs for running or riding.
strength.legs: Leg day from your split, placed so it does not hurt your key endurance sessions.
strength.runners: Runner-specific strength for hips, calves and single-leg stability.
strength.routine: Your own routine, placed so it fits around the endurance sessions.

walk.commute: Walking to work is gentle, low-impact movement – it counts a little towards your load.

steps.lthrWindow: Average heart rate of this part = threshold heart rate
steps.timeTrial: Time trial – all out, evenly paced

indoor.inclineRep: on the treadmill at the incline shown above

indoorNotes.treadmillHeat: Indoors your heart rate runs higher – no airflow, more heat. Put a fan on and go by heart rate, not speed.
indoorNotes.treadmillRamp: The belt needs a few seconds to speed up: start timing each rep once you are at speed, and slow the belt for the recoveries instead of jumping off.
indoorNotes.treadmillSplit: Long runs on the treadmill get monotonous – two halves with a short break in between are fine, the load stays the same.
indoorNotes.treadmillNoDescent: Treadmills can't go downhill, so the descents of this session are missing. If the downhill part matters, move it to a dry day instead.
indoorNotes.trainerFan: No airflow indoors: use a fan and keep a bottle in reach – your heart rate rises faster on the trainer.
indoorNotes.trainerCapped: {{indoor}} min instead of {{outdoor}} min: without coasting, trainer minutes count more. If the full ride matters, move it to another day.
indoorNotes.poolOpenWater: No sighting in the pool – lift your head every 6–8 strokes on a few lengths to keep practising it.

zwiftNotes.hrFallback: Some steps have no power target, so they were converted from heart-rate zones to a typical % FTP. Check them against your FTP in Zwift.
zwiftNotes.runPace: Zwift scales run steps to your own run pace. Easy steps are marked easier, hard steps harder – check the pace once in Zwift.
